content:
I had originally shot a series of portrait photos to test the iPhone 18 Pro's wider aperture, planning to wait until dark to see if letting in more light could shorten the capture time for Night mode shots.

I later decided to put that test on hold, because something more interesting happened: a cruise ship sailed through Tower Bridge, an extremely rare sight. It turned out to be the perfect opportunity to test the new phone's low-light video capabilities…

Over the years, the iPhone has evolved into an extremely powerful camera, but regardless of whether you're shooting photos or video, there has always been a noticeable gap in quality between daytime and nighttime results.

Apple has put a great deal of effort into low-light still photography over the years, and the results are plain to see. Measured against the standard of an extremely small sensor, today's iPhone delivers astonishing low-light performance. The addition of Night mode portrait photography in 2020 also deserves credit.

Computational photography is, broadly speaking, the key to the iPhone's low-light imaging capabilities. When we think we've taken just one photo, the phone has actually captured an entire series of frames and merged different exposures into a single image.

Video, however, is a far tougher proposition. When shooting at at least 24 frames per second, and with the scene almost always in motion, there is virtually no room to capture multiple exposures of the same frame and composite them together. That is why low-light video quality inevitably lags so far behind still photos.

That said, Apple has continued to pour enormous resources into improving this area, and each generation has delivered better low-light video performance. The 18 Pro benefits not only from Apple's year-on-year improvements to video processing, but also from a wider aperture that lets in more light. Although the increase is less than a full stop, for video every additional photon matters.

The full clip at normal speed runs to over nine minutes. I didn't want to rely on the device's excellent video stabilisation for that long, so I set up a small tripod firmly on top of the railing. I have sped the footage up to 10× normal speed, condensing it to 96 seconds, but kept a few sections at original speed so you can appreciate the painstaking precision of the tugboat's work.

How did it turn out? Not perfect, but undeniably another step forward on the path of quality evolution. Of course, someone like me can nitpick frame by frame and point out that some details look slightly soft up close, but that is very much a 'so what?' situation. An ordinary person watching this kind of video simply enjoys the spectacular scene unfolding before them, with no complaints about quality. When I look back at low-light video from a few generations ago, the difference is… night and day.

So, low-light video performance has not yet reached the level I consider ideal, but every generation improves, and this one is no exception. In fact, even in such a challenging environment, we crossed the 'good enough for most people to enjoy' threshold a long time ago.
